analysis.one_liner: Protects Utah's red rock canyon country as wilderness, barring mining, drilling, and geothermal development there.
analysis.headline: A bill to designate wilderness across ten regions of Utah drew 169 cosponsors — including 14 Republicans — but was referred to committee on May 6, 1999 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would add more than a hundred named areas across ten regions of southern and eastern Utah — canyon country around Canyonlands, Zion, the San Rafael Swell, and the Book Cliffs — to the National Wilderness Preservation System [S2][S3]. Wilderness designation is the strongest land protection in federal law: the land is withdrawn from mining claims, mineral and geothermal leasing, and sale or disposal, and motorized travel is generally barred [S3]. The bill kept existing livestock grazing in place and required the government to trade federal land for any state school-trust parcels inside the boundaries [S3]. It was introduced in May 1999, sent to the House Resources Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use and value public lands — hikers, backpackers, hunters, river runners, and the outdoor-recreation economy around Utah's canyon country — gain permanent protection of the landscapes they use. The bill also aims to protect archaeological sites on Cedar Mesa from vandalism and theft [S3]. Future generations gain because wilderness designation is permanent and the land is shielded from mining, geothermal leasing, and disposal [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Designates wilderness areas in ten regions of Utah — including Great Basin, Zion and Mojave, Grand Staircase-Escalante, Canyonlands Basin, San Rafael Swell, and Book Cliffs/Uinta Basin — as part of the National Wilderness Preservation System.
Withdraws the designated federal land from mining claims and from mineral and geothermal leasing, permanently closing it to those extractive uses except for valid rights already in existence.
Protects the Cedar Mesa archaeological area, home to cliff dwellings and rock art, which the bill says is 'in need of protection from the vandalism and theft of its unique cultural resources.'
Sets generous road setbacks (30 to 300 feet) so existing roads through canyon country remain usable, and expressly continues existing livestock grazing, keeping costs to ranchers low.
Requires the Interior Department to trade federal land of equal value for any state school-trust land inside wilderness boundaries, so Utah does not lose school-funding lands.

analysis.who_pays: Mining claimants, and oil, gas, and geothermal developers lose access to land withdrawn from entry, mining, and leasing [S3]. Off-road vehicle users lose areas that become off-limits to motorized travel under wilderness rules. Anyone holding valid existing rights is protected — the withdrawal only applies subject to rights already in place [S3]. The federal government also bears management costs, funded by appropriations the bill authorizes [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Mining, oil, gas, and off-road interests

drawbacks.text: The withdrawal from mining, mineral, and geothermal leasing permanently forecloses development of resources on roughly nine million acres, which developers and some Utah officials argued means forgone economic activity and potential revenue.
Wilderness rules bar new roads and motorized recreation inside the boundaries, reducing access for off-road vehicle users and anyone who relies on vehicle access.
Grazing can continue only at levels authorized on the day of enactment, subject to regulations the Interior Secretary considers necessary — ranchers could not expand existing operations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a classic trade-off between permanent conservation and extractive development. The costs fall on a narrow set of industries with claims to the land, and the bill deliberately softens them — existing grazing, existing roads, and existing valid rights are all preserved [S3]. The gains — permanent protection of canyon country, wildlife habitat, and archaeological sites — are diffuse but durable, and the same acreage cannot be protected later once mined or drilled. The main fair objection is that the bill is an all-or-nothing approach to land where some development interests held plans; it never went through committee deliberation where those lines could have been negotiated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Resources Committee and its National Parks subcommittee from May 1999 until the Congress ended in January 2001 — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 6, 1999 by Rep. Maurice Hinchey with 169 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Resources the same day, and on May 13, 1999 to the subcommittee on National Parks and Public Lands.
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining, oil and gas, geothermal, and off-road interests are better off because the bill died: the land remained open to mining claims, mineral and geothermal leasing, motorized recreation, and development under existing BLM management, and no permanent protection was added.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining and energy interests; the land stayed open

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 154 of 169 cosponsors — but included 14 Republicans and 1 Independent; the opposition that kept it off the floor ran through the Republican-controlled Resources Committee.

industries.note: The bill withdraws all designated land from location, entry, and patent under mining law, ending new claims on canyon country [S3]. The bill's death preserved open access for claim staking.

Designated land is withdrawn from all mineral and geothermal leasing, closing it to energy development [S3]. Had the bill passed, drilling and leasing rights on these acres would have been extinguished going forward.

The bill locks in grazing: operations authorized on the enactment date may continue indefinitely, subject to reasonable regulation [S3]. Ranchers lose room to expand or add new grazing inside wilderness, but keep what they had.

Wilderness designation bars motorized and mechanized travel inside boundaries, though the bill's generous road setbacks (as little as 30 feet) preserve existing routes and access corridors [S3]. The bill's death kept the wider landscape open to motorized use.

The bill's own findings cite hikers, campers, hunters, big-game hunting, and multi-day float trips as the uses and economy the designation protects [S3]. Permanent wilderness protects the scenery and habitat this industry depends on.
